notes.key_messages: Candidates should use a sharp pencil for plotting points and for drawing lines of best fit on graphs. This allows any errors to be easily corrected. The question might require the line of best fit to be a curve or a straight line, as appropriate. Straight lines should be drawn with a ruler, but rulers should not be used to join the points on a curve. Lines of best fit should avoid anomalous points. When requested to draw two straight intersecting lines, then a ruler must be used and there should be only two lines. When candidates are asked to compare volumes, they should look for simple relationships, such as “twice as much” or “half as much”.
notes.general_comments: The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all of the questions, and the full range of available credit was awarded. The paper discriminated successfully between candidates of different abilities but was accessible to all. No question proved to be more demanding than the others; all discriminated equally well. The majority of candidates were able to complete tables of results from readings on diagrams and plot points successfully on a grid as required in Questions 3 and 5.
notes.1a: The filter funnel was better known than the mortar.
notes.1b: Most could label the solution correctly and any of the possibilities were acceptable. There was only one acceptable answer for the solvent, however, and this proved more difficult.
notes.1ci: There were a lot of correct answers for the solvent front, but labels to every other part of the diagram were also seen.
notes.1cii: Many candidates ignored the colour that had not moved and hence the most common answer was that there were two colours present.
notes.2a: Most candidates knew that the copper oxide was black, although a lot thought that it was blue.
notes.2b: This question was well answered by the majority, showing a good understanding of the chemistry involved.
notes.2c: This answer depended on water having been identified in the part (b). Those who had correctly identified water either went on to give a correct answer, or incorrectly gave a chemical test for water.
notes.3a: The table of results was often completed correctly, with the exception of the 0.0cm point, which was actually given in the question. Many candidates recorded this point simply as 0, losing the idea of the precision of a burette. The most common error was to omit the decimal place on all readings. A large minority recorded the initial volume as 25cm . This caused problems for these candidates later in the question, although marking was based on their answers to this part.
notes.3b: Most correctly answered this part as the lack of a decimal place was not penalised again.
notes.3ci: There was a fairly even distribution between the correct colour change, which had to include colourless, and an incorrect colour change involving purple and pink.
notes.3cii: A significant number of candidates realised that an indicator was not needed because the colour change in the reaction itself was sufficient.
notes.3d: Most candidates could identify which experiment required the larger volume, but fewer realised that it was twice as much, and fewer still realised that this meant that one solution was twice as concentrated as the other.
notes.3e: There were some very good, well explained, predictions here.
notes.3f: The vast majority could explain, in simple terms, what was meant by a redox reaction.
notes.3g: Most candidates correctly gave the advantage of using a measuring cylinder as ease of use, and the disadvantage as limited accuracy.
notes.4a: As always, analysis was well known. Most realised that the filtrate would be a colourless solution.
notes.4b: Most candidates realised that there would be a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution, which would redissolve in excess.
notes.4c: Similarly, with ammonia solution, most correctly said that there would be a white precipitate which would not redissolve.
notes.4d: Nearly everyone realised that in this case there would be no white precipitate with silver nitrate solution.
notes.4e: A white precipitate with barium nitrate solution was correctly given by almost all candidates.
notes.4g: Nearly all candidates correctly identified carbon dioxide.
notes.4h: Most answers identified calcium carbonate but any Group II carbonate was accepted.
notes.5a: As always, taking readings from the thermometers was well attempted by almost all candidates.
notes.5b: This was also well answered, with the majority correctly using a ruler and drawing two lines which intersected above the highest plotted point. A significant minority either drew the lines so that they intersected at the highest plotted point, or drew a third straight line, or did not use a ruler.
notes.5c: Most could use the graph, even if it was incorrectly drawn, to work out the volume of nitric acid needed for neutralisation. °C.
notes.5d: Almost all candidates realised that room temperature was 23 (e) About half of the candidates realised that polystyrene was used because it is a good insulator. Common incorrect responses focused on the possibility of the glass beaker being broken or damaged by the heat.
notes.5f: This question differentiated well and produced some excellent answers.
notes.5g: Most realised that it was an exothermic reaction.
